## User

[2026-07-03 19:59 MDT-6] can you give me a simple script to run to regen the icon? Assume I name it's called `/Users/matthewmurphy/projects/ai-os/apps/desktop/resources/icon-og.png` but allow passing a custom input

---

## Gemini

Here is a shell script that handles the entire pipeline cleanly. It checks for a custom file argument; if you don't pass one, it automatically defaults to your icon-og.png path.


It also utilizes the /dev/null redirect we talked about so your terminal doesn't get cluttered with image processing logs.


The Script (regen-icon.sh)
Save this code into a file named regen-icon.sh in your project root:


#!/bin/bash

# Default source path
DEFAULT_SOURCE="/Users/matthewmurphy/projects/ai-os/apps/desktop/resources/icon-og.png"
TARGET_DIR="/Users/matthewmurphy/projects/ai-os/apps/desktop/resources"
TEMP_SET="$TARGET_DIR/temp.iconset"

# Use the first argument if provided, otherwise use the default path
SOURCE="${1:-$DEFAULT_SOURCE}"

# Ensure source file exists
if [ ! -f "$SOURCE" ]; then
    echo "Error: Source icon not found at $SOURCE"
    exit 1
fi

echo "Creating icon bundle from: $SOURCE"

# 1. Create a clean temporary iconset folder
rm -rf "$TEMP_SET"
mkdir -p "$TEMP_SET"

# 2. Generate mandatory sizes using sips (silencing standard output)
sips -z 16 16     "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_16x16.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 32 32     "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_16x16@2x.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 32 32     "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_32x32.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 64 64     "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_32x32@2x.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 128 128   "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_128x128.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 256 256   "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_128x128@2x.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 256 256   "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_256x256.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 512 512   "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_256x256@2x.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 512 512   "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_512x512.png" > /dev/null
sips -z 1024 1024 "$SOURCE" --out "$TEMP_SET/icon_512x512@2x.png" > /dev/null

# 3. Compile to production .icns bundle
iconutil -c icns "$TEMP_SET" -o "$TARGET_DIR/icon.icns"

# 4. Copy dev PNG copy
cp "$SOURCE" "$TARGET_DIR/icon.png"

# 5. Clean up workspace
rm -rf "$TEMP_SET"

echo "Success! Updated icon.icns and icon.png in $TARGET_DIR"


How to use it

* 
Make the script executable:


chmod +x regen-icon.sh



* 
Run it using the default path (icon-og.png):


./regen-icon.sh



* 
Run it with a custom image path:


./regen-icon.sh /path/to/some/other-image.png

{"type":"message","id":"3627b890","parentId":"ac707388","timestamp":"2026-07-04T01:39:19.941Z","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"aqfojl0e","toolName":"bash","content":[{"type":"text","text":"---\nname: verify\ndescription: Verify code changes in this repo on the right real surface. Use when the user asks to verify, test, self-test, prove something works, or when implementation is complete and verification is still needed. For `apps/desktop`, choose the correct Electron Playwright lane (`core`, `live`, or `native`), use the shared desktop helpers, rerun the owning lane for `core` and `live`, and use the targeted native spec by default for `native`.\n---\n\n# Verify\n\n## Overview\n\nProve the change works on the closest real user surface available.\n\nFor this repo, verification starts by mapping changed files to the correct package, scripts, and runtime surface instead of defaulting to the broadest or easiest test.\n\n## Workflow\n\n1. Read the closest instruction files first.\n2. Inspect the changed files and map them to the affected package and user surface.\n3. Read the current package scripts instead of assuming command names from memory.\n4. Run the smallest convincing proof first while iterating.\n5. Re-run the strongest practical lane or package-level verification before closing.\n6. Report what was verified, on which surface, and any blockers that prevented stronger proof.\n\n## Repo Map\n\n- Root rules: `AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop package: `apps/desktop/AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop test-specific rules: `apps/desktop/tests/AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop lane/setup docs: `apps/desktop/README.md`\n- Desktop command source of truth: `apps/desktop/package.json`\n\n## Desktop Verification\n\nIf changed files are under `apps/desktop`, read:\n\n- `apps/desktop/package.json`\n- `apps/desktop/README.md`\n- `apps/desktop/tests/AGENTS.md`\n\nChoose the smallest lane that matches the changed surface:\n\n- `core`\n  Background-friendly in-window Electron behavior. Default for renderer, sidebar, composer, persistence, settings, skills, and worktree UI changes.\n- `live`\n  Real provider/runtime behavior. Use when the change depends on actual runs, transcript/tool items, parallel execution, or notifications.\n- `native`\n  macOS OS-surface behavior such as pickers or real clipboard paste. Foreground-only and focus-sensitive.\n\nUse targeted specs while iterating.\nFor `core` and `live`, rerun the owning lane before closing.\nFor `native`, rerun the targeted native spec by default and expand to the full native lane only when the change touches shared native helpers, multiple native specs, or lane-wide native behavior.\n\nPrefer shared helpers in `apps/desktop/tests/helpers/electron-app.ts`.\nDo not add IPC/state shortcuts for visible behavior unless the product surface does not exist yet.\n\n## Non-Desktop Verification\n\nFor other packages, inspect the nearest `package.json`, test config, and path-scoped instructions.\nPrefer package-local typecheck and test commands over repo-wide sweeps when the change is narrow.\n\n## What To Report\n\n- Exact commands run\n- Which surface was verified\n- What user action or scenario was exercised\n- What visible or concrete result was observed\n- Any stronger proof that was blocked, and why\n\n## Gotchas\n\n- Do not stop at `pnpm test` when the changed surface is `apps/desktop`; choose the correct Electron lane explicitly.\n- Do not trust a targeted desktop spec alone if the lane matters; rerun the owning lane before closing.\n- Do not treat `native` failures as automatic product regressions. Foreground focus, picker timing, and macOS Accessibility can invalidate the run.\n- Do not force the full `native` lane for every native-adjacent change. Unrelated picker failures can hide whether the changed native surface actually works.\n- Do not add new desktop harnesses when `apps/desktop/tests/helpers/electron-app.ts` can be extended instead.\n- Do not claim real-surface proof if the test only exercised IPC, store state, or other internal plumbing.\n- Do not hard-code unstable UI details in assertions when behavior or state proves the same thing more robustly.\n\n## Close Condition\n\nDo not call the work verified until the strongest practical proof for the changed surface has passed, or the blocker is explicit and concrete.\n"}],"isError":false,"timestamp":1783129159941}}

{"type":"message","id":"8652d0ba","parentId":"054402e6","timestamp":"2026-07-04T01:56:49.554Z","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"sgeq32ly","toolName":"bash","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# JSON Event Stream Mode\n\n```bash\npi --mode json \"Your prompt\"\n```\n\nOutputs all session events as JSON lines to stdout. Useful for integrating pi into other tools or custom UIs.\n\n## Event Types\n\nEvents are defined in [`AgentSessionEvent`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-session.ts#L102):\n\n```typescript\ntype AgentSessionEvent =\n  | AgentEvent\n  | { type: \"queue_update\"; steering: readonly string[]; followUp: readonly string[] }\n  | { type: \"compaction_start\"; reason: \"manual\" | \"threshold\" | \"overflow\" }\n  | { type: \"compaction_end\"; reason: \"manual\" | \"threshold\" | \"overflow\"; result: CompactionResult | undefined; aborted: boolean; willRetry: boolean; errorMessage?: string }\n  | { type: \"auto_retry_start\"; attempt: number; maxAttempts: number; delayMs: number; errorMessage: string }\n  | { type: \"auto_retry_end\"; success: boolean; attempt: number; finalError?: string };\n```\n\n`queue_update` emits the full pending steering and follow-up queues whenever they change. `compaction_start` and `compaction_end` cover both manual and automatic compaction.\n\nBase events from [`AgentEvent`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/agent/src/types.ts#L179):\n\n```typescript\ntype AgentEvent =\n  // Agent lifecycle\n  | { type: \"agent_start\" }\n  | { type: \"agent_end\"; messages: AgentMessage[] }\n  // Turn lifecycle\n  | { type: \"turn_start\" }\n  | { type: \"turn_end\"; message: AgentMessage; toolResults: ToolResultMessage[] }\n  // Message lifecycle\n  | { type: \"message_start\"; message: AgentMessage }\n  | { type: \"message_update\"; message: AgentMessage; assistantMessageEvent: AssistantMessageEvent }\n  | { type: \"message_end\"; message: AgentMessage }\n  // Tool execution\n  | { type: \"tool_execution_start\"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string; args: any }\n  | { type: \"tool_execution_update\"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string; args: any; partialResult: any }\n  | { type: \"tool_execution_end\"; toolCallId: string; toolName: string; result: any; isError: boolean };\n```\n\n## Message Types\n\nBase messages from [`packages/ai/src/types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/ai/src/types.ts#L134):\n- `UserMessage` (line 134)\n- `AssistantMessage` (line 140)\n- `ToolResultMessage` (line 152)\n\nExtended messages from [`packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts#L29):\n- `BashExecutionMessage` (line 29)\n- `CustomMessage` (line 46)\n- `BranchSummaryMessage` (line 55)\n- `CompactionSummaryMessage` (line 62)\n\n## Output Format\n\nEach line is a JSON object. The first line is the session header:\n\n```json\n{\"type\":\"session\",\"version\":3,\"id\":\"uuid\",\"timestamp\":\"...\",\"cwd\":\"/path\"}\n```\n\nFollowed by events as they occur:\n\n```json\n{\"type\":\"agent_start\"}\n{\"type\":\"turn_start\"}\n{\"type\":\"message_start\",\"message\":{\"role\":\"assistant\",\"content\":[],...}}\n{\"type\":\"message_update\",\"message\":{...},\"assistantMessageEvent\":{\"type\":\"text_delta\",\"delta\":\"Hello\",...}}\n{\"type\":\"message_end\",\"message\":{...}}\n{\"type\":\"turn_end\",\"message\":{...},\"toolResults\":[]}\n{\"type\":\"agent_end\",\"messages\":[...]}\n```\n\n## Example\n\n```bash\npi --mode json \"List files\" 2>/dev/null | jq -c 'select(.type == \"message_end\")'\n```\n"}],"isError":false,"timestamp":1783130209554}}

## Gemini

Here is the summary of what the harness accomplished before it derailed, followed by a prompt you can use to reset its focus.


The Summary
Before falling into the testing loop, the harness successfully identified the root cause of the "New thread" bug and actually applied the fix.



* The Bug: It traced the auto-title flow from apps/desktop/electron/app-store-worktree.ts down to generateThreadTitle in packages/pi-sdk-driver/src/thread-title-generator.ts.

* The Root Cause: In thread-title-generator.ts, the code checked if (!auth.ok || !auth.apiKey) { return null; }. If you are using an authentication method that doesn't rely on a traditional API key (like an OAuth provider or local/custom auth), this strict check caused the function to silently abort and return null, leaving the thread titled "New thread".

* The Fix: The harness successfully edited thread-title-generator.ts to remove the !auth.apiKey condition (changing it to just if (!auth.ok)).


It only got stuck because it subsequently tried to prove the fix worked by writing a standalone node script, which required a complex web of mocked dependencies (AuthStorage, ModelRegistry, etc.) that it couldn't figure out how to satisfy.

{"type":"message","id":"3627b890","parentId":"ac707388","timestamp":"2026-07-04T01:39:19.941Z","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"aqfojl0e","toolName":"bash","content":[{"type":"text","text":"---\nname: verify\ndescription: Verify code changes in this repo on the right real surface. Use when the user asks to verify, test, self-test, prove something works, or when implementation is complete and verification is still needed. For `apps/desktop`, choose the correct Electron Playwright lane (`core`, `live`, or `native`), use the shared desktop helpers, rerun the owning lane for `core` and `live`, and use the targeted native spec by default for `native`.\n---\n\n# Verify\n\n## Overview\n\nProve the change works on the closest real user surface available.\n\nFor this repo, verification starts by mapping changed files to the correct package, scripts, and runtime surface instead of defaulting to the broadest or easiest test.\n\n## Workflow\n\n1. Read the closest instruction files first.\n2. Inspect the changed files and map them to the affected package and user surface.\n3. Read the current package scripts instead of assuming command names from memory.\n4. Run the smallest convincing proof first while iterating.\n5. Re-run the strongest practical lane or package-level verification before closing.\n6. Report what was verified, on which surface, and any blockers that prevented stronger proof.\n\n## Repo Map\n\n- Root rules: `AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop package: `apps/desktop/AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop test-specific rules: `apps/desktop/tests/AGENTS.md`\n- Desktop lane/setup docs: `apps/desktop/README.md`\n- Desktop command source of truth: `apps/desktop/package.json`\n\n## Desktop Verification\n\nIf changed files are under `apps/desktop`, read:\n\n- `apps/desktop/package.json`\n- `apps/desktop/README.md`\n- `apps/desktop/tests/AGENTS.md`\n\nChoose the smallest lane that matches the changed surface:\n\n- `core`\n  Background-friendly in-window Electron behavior. Default for renderer, sidebar, composer, persistence, settings, skills, and worktree UI changes.\n- `live`\n  Real provider/runtime behavior. Use when the change depends on actual runs, transcript/tool items, parallel execution, or notifications.\n- `native`\n  macOS OS-surface behavior such as pickers or real clipboard paste. Foreground-only and focus-sensitive.\n\nUse targeted specs while iterating.\nFor `core` and `live`, rerun the owning lane before closing.\nFor `native`, rerun the targeted native spec by default and expand to the full native lane only when the change touches shared native helpers, multiple native specs, or lane-wide native behavior.\n\nPrefer shared helpers in `apps/desktop/tests/helpers/electron-app.ts`.\nDo not add IPC/state shortcuts for visible behavior unless the product surface does not exist yet.\n\n## Non-Desktop Verification\n\nFor other packages, inspect the nearest `package.json`, test config, and path-scoped instructions.\nPrefer package-local typecheck and test commands over repo-wide sweeps when the change is narrow.\n\n## What To Report\n\n- Exact commands run\n- Which surface was verified\n- What user action or scenario was exercised\n- What visible or concrete result was observed\n- Any stronger proof that was blocked, and why\n\n## Gotchas\n\n- Do not stop at `pnpm test` when the changed surface is `apps/desktop`; choose the correct Electron lane explicitly.\n- Do not trust a targeted desktop spec alone if the lane matters; rerun the owning lane before closing.\n- Do not treat `native` failures as automatic product regressions. Foreground focus, picker timing, and macOS Accessibility can invalidate the run.\n- Do not force the full `native` lane for every native-adjacent change. Unrelated picker failures can hide whether the changed native surface actually works.\n- Do not add new desktop harnesses when `apps/desktop/tests/helpers/electron-app.ts` can be extended instead.\n- Do not claim real-surface proof if the test only exercised IPC, store state, or other internal plumbing.\n- Do not hard-code unstable UI details in assertions when behavior or state proves the same thing more robustly.\n\n## Close Condition\n\nDo not call the work verified until the strongest practical proof for the changed surface has passed, or the blocker is explicit and concrete.\n"}],"isError":false,"timestamp":1783129159941}}

{"type":"message","id":"8652d0ba","parentId":"054402e6","timestamp":"2026-07-04T01:56:49.554Z","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"sgeq32ly","toolName":"bash","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# JSON Event Stream Mode\n\n```bash\npi --mode json \"Your prompt\"\n```\n\nOutputs all session events as JSON lines to stdout. Useful for integrating pi into other tools or custom UIs.\n\n## Event Types\n\nEvents are defined in [`AgentSessionEvent`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-session.ts#L102):\n\n```typescript\ntype AgentSessionEvent =\n  | AgentEvent\n  | { type: \"queue_update\"; steering: readonly string[]; followUp: readonly string[] }\n  | { type: \"compaction_start\"; reason: \"manual\" | \"threshold\" | \"overflow\" }\n  | { type: \"compaction_end\"; reason: \"manual\" | \"threshold\" | \"overflow\"; result: CompactionResult | undefined; aborted: boolean; willRetry: boolean; errorMessage?: string }\n  | { type: \"auto_retry_start\"; attempt: number; maxAttempts: number; delayMs: number; errorMessage: string }\n  | { type: \"auto_retry_end\"; success: boolean; attempt: number; finalError?: string };\n```\n\n`queue_update` emits the full pending steering and follow-up queues whenever they change. `compaction_start` and `compaction_end` cover both manual and automatic compaction.\n\nBase events from [`AgentEvent`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/agent/src/types.ts#L179):\n\n```typescript\ntype AgentEvent =\n  // Agent lifecycle\n  | { type: \"agent_start\" }\n  | { type: \"agent_end\"; messages: AgentMessage[] }\n  // Turn lifecycle\n  | { type: \"turn_start\" }\n  | { type: \"turn_end\"; message: AgentMessage; toolResults: ToolResultMessage[] }\n  // Message lifecycle\n  | { type: \"message_start\"; I've investigated the codebase to see exactly how the agent works in this application and why it feels slower. 

To answer your main question: **No, it does not run individual `agy <prompt>` shell commands.** 

Instead, it uses a **Daemon RPC Architecture**:
1. The app spins up a long-running, standalone Node.js daemon process in the background.
2. Inside that daemon, it imports the core SDK (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`) natively and creates a persistent `AgentSessionRuntime` instance. 
3. When you send a prompt from the UI, the message travels through three process boundaries: Electron Renderer → Electron Main → Node.js Daemon (via TCP JSON-RPC). 

### Why is it ~30% slower?
The added latency compared to the raw `agy` CLI comes down to a few overheads:
* **Serialization across boundaries:** Every tool call, thought chunk, and output string must be serialized over JSON-RPC and Electron IPC before hitting your screen. The CLI just prints raw strings straight to `stdout`.
* **State & Metadata Management:** The `SessionSupervisor` in the GUI maintains rich session histories, threaded trees, and workspace states on disk so the GUI timeline can render perfectly.
* **Orchestration Tools:** The GUI injects an `OrchestrationRuntimeBridge` (allowing the agent to create child threads and navigate the UI). Supplying these extra tools can slightly increase token usage and "time to first token" latency.
* **Buffered Output:** The agent doesn't have a direct TTY. Output has to be buffered and piped back through the RPC connection.

I have fully documented these findings directly in the app. You can read the new documentation file here:
[docs/agent-execution-architecture.md](file:///Users/matthewmurphy/projects/ai-os/docs/agent-execution-architecture.md)

I've also committed this documentation and updated your agent work logs as per the project rules! Let me know if you want to dig deeper into optimizing any of these layers.

## Gemini

Don't abandon it just yet. If you read the second half of the output you just pasted, the agent actually found the root cause of the massive slowdown and already fixed it.


The ~30% baseline overhead is expected due to the RPC architecture and serialization, but the crippling slowness was caused by a severe I/O bottleneck. The pi-sdk-driver was executing a full JSON disk write, delete, and rename cycle for every single token the model generated. Forcing the LLM to wait for synchronous disk operations before processing the next token creates enormous backpressure, throttling the model down to your drive's sequential write speed.


The agent already modified SessionSupervisor to skip disk persistence during high-frequency streaming events (message_update and tool_execution_update), deferring the save until the message or turn completes. It also compiled the packages and documented the fix in your work logs.


Fire up the app and test it. With that synchronous disk loop removed, the latency should drop dramatically and perform much closer to your agy TUI.

## Gemini

That is a highly pragmatic pivot. It is almost always easier to port a peripheral feature into a stable core than it is to surgically rebuild a missing core inside a broken state.


When you ask an agent to "put back" missing code, it rarely performs a literal historical diff. Instead, it attempts to synthesize a brand-new implementation that satisfies the prompt while conforming to the current context of the codebase. This predictably results in the messy, hallucinated approximations you experienced.


Rolling back and porting forward is the right move. Here is how to structure that workflow so your agents don't hallucinate during the port:


1. Anchor the Baseline
Find the exact commit hash of the compiled, working antigravity build. Branch off from that point to establish your clean, high-performance foundation.


2. Deploy a Reference Worktree
Instead of constantly checking out different branches and confusing the agent's context, isolate the newer codebase. Run a git worktree add ../pi-new-features <branch-with-new-features> command. This keeps your active workspace clean while giving you and your agents concurrent read access to the newer code.


3. Constrain the Agent
When instructing your agent to pull in something like the thread forking feature, enforce strict operational boundaries.



* Point it directly at the relevant files in the reference worktree (e.g., the specific IPC handlers or UI components for forking).

* Explicitly instruct it to act as a strict transcompiler: it is to map the specific feature logic into your baseline without altering or "optimizing" the existing core execution engine.

* Require it to document its extraction plan in its work log before it writes any code.


This strategy protects your core dependencies while letting you cherry-pick the exact UI or orchestration features you actually want.


Which specific features from the newer codebase are you prioritizing for the extraction first?

## Gemini

That Error: Electron uninstall is a highly specific side effect of you using pnpm 10.


In version 10, pnpm introduced a strict security feature that completely blocks postinstall scripts from running by default.


The electron NPM package is actually just a tiny wrapper; it relies entirely on its postinstall script to reach out to GitHub and download the actual heavy macOS .zip binary. Because pnpm silently blocked that script, the binary never downloaded, and electron-vite crashes because it literally cannot find the Electron executable.


Here is how to fix it:


The Fix
You just need to authorize pnpm to run the necessary build scripts for this project.


Run this command:


pnpm approve-builds

When you run that, pnpm will update your package.json (adding an onlyBuiltDependencies array that explicitly whitelists packages like electron and esbuild).


After approving the builds, force it to actually run the blocked scripts:


pnpm rebuild

Once electron's postinstall script finishes fetching the binary, pnpm dev will boot up the app perfectly.

## Gemini

Yes, the Antigravity Agent available through the Gemini API and Antigravity CLI share the same underlying core agent harness.


They are part of the same unified ecosystem designed to provide consistent agentic capabilities—such as multi-step reasoning, tool calling, and file management—across different surfaces. Because they use a shared agent engine, improvements or updates made to this core harness generally apply to all interfaces, including the CLI, the desktop application (Antigravity 2.0), and the Gemini API agent endpoints.


While they share the same engine, they are optimized for different use cases:



* Antigravity CLI: Optimized for speed, keyboard-driven terminal workflows, and remote SSH sessions.

* Antigravity Agent (Gemini API): Designed for programmatic access, allowing you to integrate these agentic workflows directly into your own applications or services via the Interactions API.
